clue.text: Fruit found in broken crate in square

indicators.note: in places the jumbled crate inside the word for square

parts.note: nine is a square number, three times three

indicators.note: broken tells us the letters of crate are smashed and reassembled

explanation.surface: Someone finds a piece of fruit in a smashed packing crate in the town square.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' scrambles the crate's letters into ECTAR, and 'in' sets that inside the square number after its opening letter; 'found' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A smooth-skinned variety of peach is a fruit.

clue.text: One teaching about European sandpipers, primarily, or knots

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the teacher's title is read backwards

parts.note: a don is a university teacher

indicators.note: primarily means only the first letter of sandpipers is taken

explanation.surface: A teacher lectures on European sandpipers, or perhaps on knots, the birds' cousins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns DON into NOD. The knot is also a wading bird, so the surface tempts you to read 'knots' as birds; here it means tangles or bumps.
explanation.definitionFit: Nodes are swellings or joints on a stem, and a knot in wood or string is such a lump.

clue.text: Protection copper originally offered during climb

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

indicators.note: during puts one thing in the middle of another, so the letter goes inside the word for climb

parts.note: to shin up a tree is to climb it

indicators.note: originally means just the first letter of offered is used

explanation.surface: A policeman offers someone protection while they climb.
explanation.walkthrough: Copper suggests a police officer; it is the metal, symbol CU.
explanation.definitionFit: A cushion is padding that shields something from a blow, a form of protection.

clue.text: Volte-face in rating dated act?

parts.note: AB, able seaman, is a naval rating
out-of-fashion things are out
a turn is a performer's act in a variety show

explanation.surface: A sailor performs an old-fashioned stage act involving a complete reversal.
explanation.walkthrough: A rating is a non-commissioned sailor; the commonest in crosswords is AB, the able seaman.
explanation.definitionFit: A complete reversal of opinion is often called an about-turn, after the military drill command.

clue.text: Break in continuity aroused regret in miners' union

indicators.note: aroused suggests stirring up, so the letters of regret are shaken into a new order

parts.note: the NUM is Britain's National Union of Mineworkers

explanation.surface: A miners' union stirs up regret during a pause in negotiations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'aroused' turns REGRET into TERREG.
explanation.definitionFit: An interregnum is the gap between two reigns or regimes, a pause in continuous rule.

clue.text: Worry, having to take courses

explanation.surface: A worried diner works through the courses of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that worries you is eating you; to take courses at dinner is to dine.

clue.text: Model, say, initially pursued by two characters abroad

indicators.note: pursued by means the other letters go in front and the chased letter follows

parts.note: pi and nu are two letters of the Greek alphabet, characters used abroad

indicators.note: initially means only the first letter of pursued is taken

explanation.surface: A model is chased by two foreigners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' marks the model as one example of a pin-up. The two Greek letters PI and NU come first; P follows, since 'pursued by' puts it behind them.
explanation.definitionFit: A pin-up is a glamorous photograph, typically of a model, for hanging on a wall; 'say' marks it as an example.

clue.text: Specially trained horse, one in Puerto Rico

indicators.note: in places the card for one inside the two-letter abbreviation

parts.note: PR is the postal abbreviation for Puerto Rico
an ace counts as one in cards

explanation.surface: A horse trained for a special purpose is the best one in Puerto Rico.
explanation.definitionFit: A pacer is a horse bred and trained to move both legs on one side together, for harness racing.

clue.text: Possibly 27 can upset religious observance

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so the word for can is read backwards

parts.note: a tin is a can
a rite is a religious ceremony

explanation.surface: A tin can is knocked over during a religious ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: 27 refers to the answer to 27 across, ESTER; 'upset' turns TIN into NIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Compounds such as amyl nitrite are esters of nitrous acid, so this is one possible example.

clue.text: Pole swallows most of meal with great speed

parts.note: a post is a pole
to have a drink is to swallow it

indicators.note: most of means the word for meal loses its last letter

parts.note: tea is an evening meal in Britain

explanation.surface: A Polish diner bolts most of a meal very quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: Pole looks like a Polish person; it is a post. 'swallows' looks like a container signal, but here it means consumes, as in having a meal. 'most of' drops the final letter of the meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Posthaste is an old idiom for doing something immediately and very fast.

clue.text: Play about princess left by aeschylus in the end

parts.note: Di is the familiar name of Princess Diana

indicators.note: in the end means the final letter of the Greek dramatist's name

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: A play about a princess abandoned by the Greek tragedian Aeschylus at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play about' looks like a stage work on a subject; it is the verb 'frolic'.
explanation.definitionFit: To disport oneself is to frolic, to play around merrily.

clue.text: One involved in diplomacy meets American historian

indicators.note: involved in puts the numeral inside the word for diplomacy

parts.note: tact is diplomatic skill
I is the Roman numeral one
US is short for American, as in the United States

explanation.surface: A diplomat meets an American historian.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacitus was the Roman writer of the Annals and Histories, a historian of the early empire.

clue.text: Wading bird's singular colour

parts.note: S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular
a tint is a shade of colour

explanation.surface: A wading bird has unusual colouring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'singular' looks like 'remarkable'; it is the grammar abbreviation S.
explanation.definitionFit: The stint is a small sandpiper, a shore bird that wades.

clue.text: Do up short red coat by mistake

indicators.note: short means the word red is cut off before its last letter

parts.note: an animal's fur is its coat
bish is British slang for a blunder

explanation.surface: Someone renovates a cropped red jacket by accident.
explanation.walkthrough: BISH is informal British slang for a mistake. The surface wants an anagram of 'short red coat'; there are too many letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To do up a house is to renovate it, to make it like new.

clue.text: Fine even Rachel, surprisingly, for unauthorised absence

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencil leads

indicators.note: surprisingly signals the letters of even Rachel turning up in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: Even Rachel is fined, to everyone's surprise, for going absent without leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surprisingly' scrambles the two words into RENCHLEAVE, placed after the abbreviation for fine. Rachel is just a name chosen for its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking French leave is an idiom for slipping away without permission.

clue.text: Team supporter in cooler?

explanation.surface: A football supporter sits in the cool box.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of a team is an enthusiast; a device that blows air cools a room.

clue.text: Number historically supporting grievance about university

indicators.note: about means going round, so the word for supporting wraps the university letter

parts.note: to be for something is to support it
a score is a grudge, as in settling an old score

explanation.surface: A historical number supports a grievance concerning a university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts U inside FOR, giving FOUR.
explanation.definitionFit: Fourscore is an archaic way of saying eighty, so a number used in older texts.

clue.text: Economise? Head shows incompetence

parts.note: to economise is to consume less, read as two words
a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness or Sheerness

explanation.surface: A boss urges cost-cutting, which only shows how inept they are.
explanation.walkthrough: NESS is a headland, found in British place names.
explanation.definitionFit: Being of no use is ineptness, a lack of the skill required.

clue.text: Legal adviser thus permitted to accompany men

parts.note: so means thus
licit means lawful or allowed
OR, other ranks, are soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: A lawyer is thereby allowed to go along with the soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: OR, other ranks, is the military term for enlisted men.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a solicitor is the lawyer who gives legal advice to clients.

clue.text: A council nan organised, contrary to church law

indicators.note: organised suggests putting into new order, so the letters of a council nan are rearranged

explanation.surface: A grandmother arranges a council meeting in defiance of church rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organised' rearranges A COUNCIL NAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Canon law is church law, so anything not in accordance with the canons breaks it.

clue.text: Sign of omission restricting degree holder's floor show

indicators.note: restricting means hemming in, so the caret mark encloses the degree

parts.note: a caret is the mark used to show where something left out should be inserted
a BA, Bachelor of Arts, holds a degree

explanation.surface: A missing graduate's name is noted at a nightclub show.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabaret is entertainment performed in a nightclub or restaurant while the audience dines.

clue.text: Bring action against flipping London station? Not half

indicators.note: flipping means turning over, so the remaining letters are read backwards
not half means only half the station name survives, the other three letters dropped

parts.note: Euston is a main railway terminus in London

explanation.surface: Someone wants to sue a London railway station, angry at its service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half' drops TON from EUSTON, leaving EUS, and 'flipping' turns that to SUE. 'flipping' also reads as a mild British swear word.
explanation.definitionFit: To sue someone is to bring a lawsuit, a legal action, against them.

clue.text: Country fellow is consuming game served up

indicators.note: served up in a down clue means turned upwards, so everything is read backwards

parts.note: a fellow is a man

indicators.note: consuming means eating up, so is takes in the game

parts.note: RU is rugby union

explanation.surface: A local man devours game that has been served to him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'consuming' puts the rugby abbreviation inside 'is'. 'served up' then turns the whole run, MANIRUS, upwards, as fits a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Surinam, now usually spelled Suriname, is a South American nation.

clue.text: Unintelligent son extremely uncivil about Bellini's first opera

indicators.note: about means going round, so the outer letters surround the rest
extremely means the outermost letters of uncivil
first means the opening letter of the composer's name

parts.note: Norma is an opera by Bellini

explanation.surface: A rude son complains about Bellini's first opera, to show how dim he is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' gives the first and last letters of 'uncivil', and 'about' wraps them round the composer's initial and his opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Subnormal means below average intelligence, a dated term for being dim.

clue.text: Basket-maker socks retailer in east end

indicators.note: in the East End of London Cockneys drop their aitches, so the opening letter goes

parts.note: a hosier sells socks and stockings

explanation.surface: A man who weaves baskets sells socks in the East End.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys, from London's East End, traditionally drop the H sound at the start of words.
explanation.definitionFit: Osier is willow whose pliant shoots are woven into baskets.

clue.text: Calcareous substance fellow artist found by lake

parts.note: co- as a prefix means fellow, as in co-worker
RA, Royal Academician, is a British artist

explanation.surface: A painter colleague is found beside a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: CO plus RA read together as 'fellow artist', co-Royal Academician.
explanation.definitionFit: Coral is the hard skeletal material made of calcium carbonate built by marine polyps.

clue.text: One may bear fruit — but not if it's the answer!

definitions.text: One may bear fruit — but not if it's the answer!

parts.words: One may bear fruit — but not if it's the answer!
parts.note: a citrus tree bears its own yellow fruit, yet the same word for a dud or flop is something that never bears fruit in the figurative sense of succeeding

explanation.surface: A tree may produce fruit, but a failure does not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bear fruit' is used both literally, of a citrus tree, and figuratively, of plans succeeding; a dud product is called by the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: A dud or failed venture, which by definition does not succeed, is called this citrus name.

clue.text: Swimmer runs in like an oik

indicators.note: in places the runs letter inside the word for loutish

parts.note: an oik is a lout, so behaving like one is oafish
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A swimmer rushes in like an uncouth lout.
explanation.walkthrough: An oik is British slang for a crude, ill-mannered person.
explanation.definitionFit: The oarfish is a long ribbon-like deep-sea fish, a swimmer.

clue.text: Swindles and cheats on a regular basis

indicators.note: on a regular basis means taking every other letter, here the second, fourth and sixth

explanation.surface: Someone routinely swindles and cheats.
explanation.definitionFit: To have someone is slang for tricking or conning them.

clue.text: Not many working? It means the opposite

indicators.note: working means set in motion, so the letters of not many are rearranged

explanation.surface: Few people have jobs; the phrase means its reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'working' turns NOT MANY into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A word with an opposite sense to another, like hot to cold, is its counterpart in meaning.

clue.text: Organic compound identified in old book on radio

indicators.note: on radio means heard rather than seen, so the book's name is said aloud

parts.note: Esther is a book of the Old Testament

explanation.surface: An organic chemical is identified in an Old Testament book read on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: The H of the Old Testament book's name is silent, so the two words sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Esters are organic chemicals formed from an acid and an alcohol, often fruity smelling.

clue.text: Course director in south island always dipping into Eliot?

indicators.note: in places the poet's initials and their contents between the two outer pieces

parts.note: the Isle of Man is in the Irish Sea

indicators.note: dipping into means going inside, so always enters the poet's initials

parts.note: TS are the initials of the poet T. S. Eliot
e'er is a poetic contraction of ever, meaning always

explanation.surface: A course director on a southern island is forever immersed in Eliot's poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dipping into' puts the poetic word for always inside the poet's initials, giving TEERS, and 'in' sets that between the compass point and the island.
explanation.definitionFit: A steersman is the one who steers a vessel, directing its course.
